rationale: Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t clearly separate them (PGS002054 only shows a small partial-r=0.0144; PGS000753 provides an OR per SD of 1.37, which is at least interpretable as moderate PRS signal). The key differentiator is study archetype/endpoint fidelity: PGS000753 comes from a disease-focused AAA genetic architecture study (MVP/Mayo) with a clearly stated prevalent AAA endpoint, whereas PGS002054 is from a UK Biobank portability framework paper where per-trait scores are not disease-optimized. Despite PGS002054’s stronger method/variant coverage (LDpred2, genome-wide), the framework-origin plus lack of stronger comparable performance evidence makes it less well-supported than the disease-focused PGS000753.

PGS002738 is the better match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is explicitly Alcohol use disorder with trait_efo exactly mapped to alcohol dependence, whereas PGS000201 is centered on “Problematic alcohol use” and uses a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is a more quantitative/problem-use phenotype and less directly a dependence diagnosis. Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared on the preferred PRS-comparable metrics; in that setting, PGS002738’s stronger reported stratification (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96) provides more supportive discrimination evidence than PGS000201’s modest ΔR²=0.01192. Both are EUR-evaluated with similar validation N (~7.9k vs ~7.6k) and same method (PRS-CS), so the decision is driven mainly by endpoint fidelity plus stronger effect-size evidence for PGS002738.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) at trait_reported/trait_efo, but PGS000753 has cleaner endpoint/covariate transparency and more PRS-comparable evidence: it specifies a prevalent AAA case-control phenotype and uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and it reports a PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.37, moderate signal). PGS003972 is methodologically/structurally stronger on paper (PRS-CS with ~1.1M variants; large multi-cohort meta-analysis context), but its only visible discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.69 with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect size, which is not comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given the domain guidance to not substitute full-model AUROC for PRS performance, PGS000753 is better-supported on the visible fields despite being sparser.

PGS004913 is better supported for the target because it is explicitly disease-focused on alcohol-associated cirrhosis in heavy drinkers (publication title and cohorts GenomALC/NIAAA), with tight endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis) and provides PRS-relevant effect evidence (OR top vs bottom deciles = 4.4). PGS000704, while mapping to the same EFO term, comes from a broad UKB biomarker genetics framework paper and only reports a full-model C-index (0.711) plus a modest HR (1.18), with no PRS-only metrics; the full-model metric is not comparable as PRS performance and is likely covariate-influenced. Both use only basic covariates and are largely EUR-evaluated, but the disease-specific design and stronger PRS effect separation favor PGS004913.

PGS001267 is the better match to the target trait as a generic ankylosing spondylitis diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) endpoint (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)”, phenotyping_reported “TTE ankylosing spondylitis”), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease-risk target. The two records are otherwise near-clones (same UKB-only framework paper, same snpnet method, 10 variants, same covariates, same training N and validation N, same ancestry distribution), and while PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-only AUC/R2 (0.7346/0.1023 vs 0.7265/0.0988), that small metric edge does not outweigh the cleaner endpoint alignment of PGS001267.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it has exact trait alignment (trait_reported and trait_efo both aortic stenosis) and endpoint fidelity (incident aortic stenosis cases). It also shows stronger PRS signal via effect size (HR=1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255). While PGS005252 reports a full-model C-index=0.87, its covariates are much heavier (multiple comorbidities and BMI/smoking/renal failure), so that discrimination is likely covariate-driven and not directly comparable; however PGS005255 provides no AUC/R2 at all either, so metrics don’t rescue it. PGS005255 additionally has weaker phenotype labeling (trait_reported is mean pressure gradient; trait_efo includes aortic measurement), making it less directly faithful to the disease endpoint despite mentioning incident aortic stenosis. Given similar EUR-only development/evaluation, the stronger endpoint alignment and higher HR favor PGS005252.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with very large variant count (326,000) and a slightly stronger reported discrimination proxy (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51]) than PGS002739 (OR 1.76 [1.32–2.34]). PGS002739 is a gene-based PRS-CSx model with only 858 variants and AFR-only evaluation; while valuable for African American deployment, the sparse gene-based construction provides less polygenic coverage and its effect-size evidence is weaker here. Validation sample sizes are similar (7,900 vs 6,315) and covariates are unknown for both, so they don’t differentiate.

PGS001777 is better supported for the specific target endpoint because it comes from a disease-focused study explicitly about predicting alcohol-related cirrhosis in drinkers and reports strong PRS effect evidence (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18; β=1.132), whereas PGS000704 is from a broad biomarker genetics framework paper and its PRS signal appears modest (HR=1.18). Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model discrimination (0.671 vs 0.711) is not a reliable cross-model differentiator; in that setting, the stronger endpoint-focused evidence and materially larger genetic effect sizes favor PGS001777 despite its smaller variant count and unknown covariates.

PGS005052 is better supported for angina pectoris because it uses a direct diagnosis-style endpoint (PheCode 411.3; phenotyping_reported: Angina pectoris) and comes from a disease-focused multi-population PRS methods paper with MVP development and multi-ancestry GWAS/evaluation context, plus it reports a reasonably strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.491). In contrast, PGS001261 is from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event phenotype (TTE angina pectoris), which domain guidance flags as a weaker archetype for external reliability; its PRS-only metrics are available but modest (PGS-only AUROC 0.582, R2 0.012) and largely indicate limited standalone PRS signal despite a higher covariate-driven full-model AUROC. Overall, PGS005052 has stronger endpoint fidelity and more credible PRS signal evidence (OR) than the framework TTE score.

PGS002739 is the more endpoint-faithful match to the target trait alcohol dependence: it has trait_efo="alcohol dependence" and phenotyping_reported="Alcohol use disorder" (a direct diagnostic endpoint), whereas PGS000201 is framed as "Problematic alcohol use" with an alcohol-dependence-measurement EFO and a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is closer to a severity/measurement phenotype than a clean case-control AUD endpoint. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparison relies on available effect-size evidence: PGS002739 provides a clear case-control stratification metric (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76), while PGS000201 reports only ΔR²=0.01192 and a beta on a transformed count outcome, which is less directly comparable to alcohol dependence risk. Although PGS000201 has cleaner disclosed covariates and far more variants (genome-wide PRS-CS), PGS002739’s stronger endpoint alignment and more interpretable risk-discrimination evidence outweigh the covariate-unknown penalty here.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and neither provides a PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS003972 is better supported by study archetype and construction: it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many external cohorts listed) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with larger variant coverage (1,118,997 vs 592,187). Its reported AUROC=0.69 is full-model and thus not PRS-comparable, but it is at least a concrete discrimination metric, whereas PGS002054 (a UKB portability framework score) reports only a small partial-r (0.0144) and is more likely to be a generic framework-derived model despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation. Given the domain guidance that disease-focused multi-cohort models typically outperform portability-framework scores absent clearly superior PRS-only metrics, PGS003972 is preferred.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper, with identical covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and the same DEV/EVAL ancestry distribution, so the decision rests on endpoint fidelity and PRS-only metrics. PGS001262 uses a direct doctor-diagnosed angina phenotype ("Vascular/heart problems diagnosed by doctor Angina"), which is a straightforward disease-status endpoint for the target trait, whereas PGS001261 is explicitly time-to-event (TTE), a mild endpoint mismatch/packaging for a generic angina pectoris target. On comparable PRS-only performance, PGS001262 is slightly better (PGS-only AUROC 0.5868; R2 0.01304) than PGS001261 (0.5823; 0.01228), and both are plausible under the heritability ceiling. Training/validation size differences are weak tie-breakers here, so the cleaner endpoint plus marginally stronger PRS-only metrics favor PGS001262.

Both candidates have exact endpoint fidelity for ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). PGS001267 is better supported on directly PRS-comparable performance: it reports PGS-only AUROC=0.7265 and PGS-only R²=0.0988 in Europeans, whereas PGS002089 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919) and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its predictive strength harder to judge. Although PGS002089 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants (22,026) and includes some non-EUR evaluation (EUR/GME/SAS), the lack of standard PRS-only metrics leaves weaker visible evidence than PGS001267’s explicit PRS-only discrimination/variance explained.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it has direct concept alignment (trait_reported and trait_efo both “aortic stenosis”) and the same endpoint as its sibling (phenotyping_reported: incident aortic stenosis) with similarly clean basic covariates. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either candidate, the main differentiators are endpoint fidelity and effect-size/scale signals: PGS005254 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53 for PGS005255) and is trained on a larger sample (205,483 vs 98,645), while PGS005255’s trait_reported (“Mean pressure gradient”) and broader trait_efo (“aortic stenosis, aortic measurement”) are less directly disease-endpoint faithful for an aortic stenosis risk score.

PGS001135 has clearer, PRS-comparable performance evidence for the broad target trait arthritis: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.539) and PGS-only R2 (0.00291), with basic covariates and a heritability-consistent R2 (well below the provided h2_liability ceiling). It also includes multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), supporting some transportability context. In contrast, PGS004477 is mapped to arthritis but is a narrower endpoint (“M13 (Other arthritis)”) and provides no AUROC/R2 at all (only a modest OR≈1.20) with covariates listed as unknown, making its PRS strength and comparability harder to judge despite its genome-wide LDpred2 construction and larger variant count.

PGS002089 has cleaner endpoint fidelity to the target trait (phenotyping_reported is simply “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event/incident-style endpoint (“TTE ankylosing spondylitis”), which domain guidance flags as a weaker match for a generic disease-risk target when competing with a direct diagnosis endpoint. Structurally, PGS002089 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (22,026 vs 10), which is generally more robust than the very sparse snpnet model from the known pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”), a study archetype cautioned to generalize less well. Although PGS001268 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.7346/0.1023), that advantage is tempered by the framework/sparse-model warning and the endpoint mismatch; PGS002089’s lack of PRS-only AUROC/R² lowers certainty but does not outweigh its stronger phenotype alignment and method/coverage signals.

PGS004913 is the better-supported standalone PRS for alcoholic liver cirrhosis because its endpoint fidelity is cleaner and its evaluation appears PRS-focused: phenotyping_reported matches the target directly (“Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis”) with basic covariates (age, sex, PCs) and a disease-focused PRS publication specifically about cirrhosis risk among heavy drinkers. Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R², it reports a PRS effect size (OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4) and an R² value (0.029) without obvious clinical-risk packaging. In contrast, PGS001777 comes from a paper explicitly combining a genetic risk score with diabetes, reports only a full-model AUROC (0.671) with unknown covariates (so the AUROC is not PRS-comparable and may be covariate-driven), and its phenotyping_reported is partially mismatched/restricted (“Cirrhosis (males)”). Both are EUR-only, but PGS004913 has the more coherent trait/phenotype alignment and less risk of non-genetic packaging confounding.

PGS001135 is better supported on-record for the broad target trait “arthritis”: it matches the same EFO term and uses a generic arthritis endpoint (“Arthritis (nos)”) with clearly stated phenotyping and basic covariates, and it reports clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.539 and PGS-only R2=0.00291) that are sanity-consistent with the provided low heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS004547 targets a narrower/administrative subtype label (“M13 (Other arthritis)”) and appears to be a risk-factor integration/metaPRS package (method_name RFDiseasemetaPRS) with unknown covariates and no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported (only OR=1.26, which is weak-to-moderate). Despite PGS001135 coming from a pan-trait UKB framework paper, the substantially stronger and cleaner performance evidence plus broader multi-ancestry evaluation support make it the more defensible choice here.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo=angina pectoris). PGS001262 provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.58683; PGS-only R2=0.01304) with basic covariates and a heritability-sane R2 (below the provided h2_obs ceiling), plus broader multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). In contrast, PGS005052 reports only a full-model C-index (0.766) with no PGS-only AUC/R2, so its discrimination is not directly attributable to the PRS; while it has a supportive OR per SD (~1.49) and a genome-wide LDpred construction, the lack of PRS-only metrics makes its PRS strength less well-supported on the visible fields. Net: PGS001262 is better-supported by directly comparable PRS-only evidence despite being from a pan-trait UKB framework paper.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo = aortic stenosis; incident case phenotyping; EUR-only dev/eval) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on effect-size evidence and design comparability. PGS005254 shows a clear PRS association with HR=1.64 (95% CI 1.50–1.78) under relatively basic covariate adjustment (age, age^2, sex, PCs), making the genetic signal more interpretable as PRS-driven. PGS005252 reports a higher HR (1.92) but pairs it with a very covariate-heavy model (multiple cardiometabolic comorbidities and BMI/smoking/renal failure) and only a full-model C-index/AUC=0.87, which is likely dominated by clinical covariates and is not PRS-comparable; it also lacks CI for the HR. Given the cleaner covariate context and more self-contained PRS effect reporting, PGS005254 is better-supported on the visible fields despite smaller validation N.

PGS000327 is clearly better supported for the target autism spectrum disorder because its endpoint fidelity is direct and coherent across fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all = autism spectrum disorder), and it comes from a disease-focused ASD GWAS meta-analysis context with explicit training (n=28,592) and a larger validation sample (n=7,148) plus a meaningful effect size (OR=1.33). In contrast, PGS002790 has an explicit phenotype mismatch (phenotyping_reported = "Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)"), unclear training sample size (N/A), and only a small partial R² (0.00546) reported as a full-model/partial metric rather than a clean PRS-only metric; despite a more polygenic method/variant count, the endpoint mismatch and weaker/less interpretable performance evidence make it less reliable for ASD.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and have similarly light, non-leaky covariates and identical EUR evaluation size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. In this metric-tied setting, PGS002755 is structurally better supported as a standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants versus PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNPs, which is generally more appropriate for a polygenic disease like atopic eczema. PGS002755 also shows a slightly stronger HR (1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587’s multi-cohort training list (EB/FinnGen/UKB) is supportive but not enough to outweigh the much sparser construction and weaker effect size given otherwise near-identical endpoint and evaluation context.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping alignment to basal cell carcinoma, same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes (training n=11,734; validation n=11,322), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC=0.632 is not a differentiator. The only visible performance edge is slightly higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.79 vs 3.61) for PGS000454 compared with PGS000452, making PGS000454 marginally better supported, but the difference is small hence low confidence.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the target trait atrial flutter because it is an exact endpoint match (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and it reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R2=0.025), with basic covariates and an R2 that is plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling context. In contrast, PGS002050 uses a broader combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”), and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial correlation is provided), making its predictive performance less directly comparable for atrial flutter specifically despite larger training size and a genome-wide variant set.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to basal cell carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.64 for PGS000119 vs 0.632 for PGS000454) is not a reliable PRS discriminator. Covariates are similarly basic (age/sex/batch/PCs) and both are EUR-only with MGI development. PGS000454 is slightly better-supported on the visible record because it provides a richer performance package beyond AUROC (Nagelkerke R², Brier score, top-1% OR, and beta/SE) while maintaining similar per-SD OR (~1.66 vs ~1.65). PGS000119’s larger validation N and marginally higher full-model AUROC are weak tie-breakers here. Overall this is near-tied, hence low confidence.

PGS004587 is the better-supported match to the generic target trait “atopic eczema” because its endpoint is a direct, general disease incidence phenotype (“Incident atopic dermatitis”) in a very large European evaluation sample (n=337,910), and it reports a PRS-stratified effect size (HR high vs low PRS = 1.153, 95% CI 1.037–1.282) without obvious clinical-risk packaging. In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (“Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis”), has a much smaller validation sample (n=676), and its only strong-looking metrics are full-model AUROC/R² (0.93/0.49) with covariates including parental ethnicity—these are not PRS-only metrics and the very high R² is not directly comparable (and is implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling), making its apparent performance advantage unreliable for PRS ranking.

PGS002727 is better supported for the target asthma endpoint because it comes from a disease-focused pediatric asthma PRS study and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.57, 95% CI 1.55–1.60), whereas PGS001782 is from a global biobank portability/framework paper and provides only modest PRS-comparable performance (Nagelkerke R2 covariates-regressed-out 0.048844) with limited single-record evaluation. Although PGS001782 has a clean PRS-comparable R2 and basic covariates (sex/age/PCs), its framework archetype is a negative signal when a disease-focused asthma model exists; PGS002727 also shows broader multi-ancestry evaluation coverage and much larger validation support (n=391,820 vs n=7,128), even if its reported AUROC/R2 are full-model and covariates are unknown. Overall, the combination of endpoint-focused study context plus strong OR evidence favors PGS002727 over the framework-derived PGS001782.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable as PRS evidence. PGS005168 is heavily packaged with a named clinical risk calculator covariate (CHARGE-AF) in addition to age/sex/array, making its high full-model C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and weak evidence about standalone PRS quality. PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that risk-wrapper leakage, and still shows strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.94), which is meaningful PRS signal. Although PGS005168 has a more polygenic method/variant count (PRS-CS; 382,963 variants) and larger EUR validation, the CHARGE-AF packaging is a stronger negative for PRS comparability than those structural advantages are positive here.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model discrimination is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. PGS005168’s very high C-index (0.8718) is heavily discounted because covariates include the named clinical risk calculator CHARGE-AF (risk-wrapper packaging), making the reported performance likely covariate-driven and less informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that packaging concern, and it also shows strong PRS effect size evidence (OR 1.82 per SD) alongside a genome-wide cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with much larger variant count. Overall, PGS005313 has cleaner evaluation context and stronger structural/effect-size support than PGS005168’s clinically packaged model.

PGS001263 is the better-supported match for the target trait (atrial flutter) because its endpoint is directly atrial flutter across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS001339 explicitly bundles atrial fibrillation + flutter and uses a time-to-event phenotype (TTE), reducing endpoint fidelity for a generic atrial flutter target. Both are from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical training size, covariates, and validation N, so design/transportability are essentially tied; performance is also very similar, but PGS001263 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC (0.617 vs 0.613) and PRS-only R2 (0.02517 vs 0.02447), both well below the heritability ceiling, giving it a small empirical edge on top of the cleaner phenotype match.

Both candidates target the same combined endpoint (trait_efo includes atrial flutter; trait_reported is atrial fibrillation and flutter), but PGS001339 has clearer PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports PGS-only AUROC=0.613 and PGS-only R2=0.02447 (no covariates), which is interpretable and stays below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0157; noting scale differences, it is at least not wildly implausible). PGS002050 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.1034) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making cross-model PRS discrimination harder to judge. While PGS002050 has a stronger structural method/coverage signal (LDpred2 with 554,908 variants vs snpnet with 2,142) and larger training N, the lack of directly comparable PRS-only metrics and reliance on a portability-framework context leaves it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS001339’s explicit PRS-only evaluation.

PGS001782 is the stronger choice on study archetype and structural plausibility: it comes from a global multi-biobank PRS development/benchmarking context with a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) and very large variant coverage (884,043), and reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2=0.048844) on an asthma endpoint that matches the target. PGS001344 has slightly higher reported PRS-only metrics in EUR (PGS-only R2=0.05973; AUROC=0.64568) and larger validation n, but it is explicitly from the pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse snpnet framework (a known underperforming archetype for external generalization) with a very sparse 6,139-variant model; its apparent metric edge is modest and not enough to outweigh the framework+sparse-method penalty relative to the multi-cohort genome-wide score. Both have acceptable endpoint fidelity (doctor-diagnosed vs generic asthma), and both use only basic covariates, so the decision hinges mainly on framework vs multi-cohort design and method/coverage.

Both candidates have perfect endpoint fidelity to basal cell carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), similar basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PC1-4), same EUR-only context, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC differences are not a reliable PRS discriminator). PGS000452 has slightly stronger supporting evidence on the visible record: it reports additional performance detail beyond AUROC (Nagelkerke R², Brier score, and top-1% vs rest OR=3.61) and has a marginally higher per-SD effect size (OR 1.663 vs 1.65 for PGS000119), while PGS000119’s main advantage is larger validation N and a trivially higher full-model AUROC (0.64 vs 0.632), which is weak and likely noise given both are full-model. Overall edge to PGS000452, but the records are near-tied.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation size (n=19,924). Performance evidence is also essentially identical (partial-r 0.0716 with overlapping CIs) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. With metrics and phenotype tied, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002032 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (19,768 variants) versus PGS001824’s very sparse penalized regression score (22 variants), which is less likely to capture polygenic signal for this trait. Hence PGS002032 is better-supported on method/variant-count grounds, though confidence is only moderate because the observed performance is indistinguishable.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.78 in PGS005313 vs 0.74 in PGS002814) are only weakly informative. PGS005313 is better-supported structurally and for transportability: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with far more variants (1,271,239 vs 4,520) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (European, African, South Asian, East Asian, Hispanic/LatAm, Other) rather than EAS-only evaluation for PGS002814. Effect-size evidence is strong for both (OR 1.82 vs 1.94), but PGS002814’s reported Nagelkerke R2=0.14 is not clearly PRS-only and is high relative to the AF heritability ceiling context, making it less clean as comparative evidence. Overall, PGS005313 has the stronger multi-ancestry, genome-wide PRS evidence package, while PGS002814 is more limited to EAS evaluation with a sparse P+T construction.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis), same EFO mapping (arthritis), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and size (n=174,489), same EUR-only development/evaluation, same variant count (1,059,939), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so metrics cannot differentiate via clean PRS-comparable discrimination). The main differentiator is the available PRS signal proxy: PGS004547 reports a higher per-SD effect size (OR 1.262) than PGS004477 (OR 1.196), indicating stronger discriminative power given otherwise identical metadata. Method-wise, PGS004547’s RFDiseasemetaPRS suggests an aggregated/meta-PRS construction, which is a mild positive structural signal versus the single-score LDpred2 in PGS004477 when endpoints and evidence are otherwise tied.

PGS001824 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported both specifically "Disorders of bilirubin excretion" mapped to bilirubin metabolism disease), whereas PGS000924 uses a broader combined phenotype and a time-to-event definition ("disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism (TTE)") that is less faithful to the generic target disease concept. Although PGS000924 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC/R², those values (PGS-only R²=0.218) exceed the provided heritability ceiling estimate for bilirubin-related traits (h2_obs≈0.089), making the metric plausibly non-comparable/mis-scaled and reducing its evidentiary value. PGS002755 is a closer match to the target trait as a general atopic dermatitis/atopic eczema endpoint (incident atopic dermatitis) and is built as a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than PGS001773’s 25-variant GWAS-hit score targeting the narrower subtype “moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis.” Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS001773’s very high AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 are full-model metrics with covariates including parental ethnicity and are not comparable PRS evidence and are also implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling, so they should be heavily discounted.
