Given the stronger disease-focused multi-ancestry validation context and strong OR/HR evidence, PGS003725 edges PGS000013 despite missing explicit PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS004254 is the stronger Crohn’s disease match on endpoint fidelity and structural PRS design: it targets Crohn’s disease directly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both Crohn’s disease) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,682), which is generally more appropriate for a polygenic autoimmune disease than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001330 (220 variants) from a known pan-trait UKB framework paper. Although PGS001330 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.5759; PGS-only R² 0.00621, below the h2_obs ceiling ~0.0122) and has multi-ancestry evaluation, it is explicitly a time-to-event phenotype and its modest PRS-only performance plus framework archetype make it less compelling than the disease-focused Crohn’s diagnosis endpoint with strong per-SD effect size evidence in PGS004254 (OR 2.18). PGS004254’s reported AUROC is full-model (0.72) and not PRS-comparable, so confidence is not high, but overall the endpoint + method/coverage + effect-size package outweighs PGS001330’s modest PRS-only metrics.

PGS002237 is better supported for the target trait CKD because its endpoint is more specific and clinically anchored (stage 3+ with eGFR <45), and it comes from a CKD-focused cross-ancestry prediction study with multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE), suggesting broader transportability than PGS004158’s EUR/SAS-only evaluation. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable; however, PGS002237 at least shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.47 vs 1.39) and a more coherent disease-focused evidence package. PGS004158 is from a methods/biobank-variation benchmarking paper with a broader phenotype definition (“CKD or dialysis”) and offers no covariate context beyond ‘0’, making its modest full-model AUROC (~0.59) less informative for PRS quality than the disease-focused, multi-ancestry-supported PGS002237.

Both candidates match the target trait well (all-cause dementia; EFO dementia), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004281 (0.819 vs 0.761) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage. PGS005170 is better-supported structurally and for transportability: it is an explicit integrative/ensemble PRS (24 component PRSs; >1.3M variants) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR) plus an effect-size signal (HR per SD 1.25), whereas PGS004281 is a very sparse 110-variant single-UKB GenoBoost score with EUR-only evaluation and no effect sizes. PGS005170’s covariates include APOE ε2/ε4 dosage (a mild comparability concern), but PGS004281’s apparent metric edge is still only full-model and thus not decisive; overall evidence package favors PGS005170.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo=major depressive disorder; EUR GWAS/EVAL; similar genome-wide PRS-CS family and ~1.09M variants). However, PGS002759 provides a cleaner PRS-specific performance signal via an effect size (OR per SD=1.26, 95% CI 1.22–1.30) with explicitly basic covariates (age, sex, 10 PCs, technical), whereas PGS003333 reports only a full-model Nagelkerke pseudo-R2=0.022 (not PRS-only) with covariates listed as unknown, making its performance evidence less directly interpretable for standalone PRS quality. Validation sample sizes are similar (39,444 vs 34,703), so the effect-size evidence and clearer covariate disclosure tip the balance to PGS002759.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Cirrhosis”). Neither provides a clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC cannot be used as a decisive PRS metric (PGS004621’s AUROC=0.68 is full-model with age/sex/PCs only). With PRS-comparable metrics absent for both, structural/study-design signals dominate: PGS004621 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and is developed/validated across a large multi-cohort biobank set with very large EUR evaluation (n=1,153,995), whereas PGS000726 is a sparse 12-variant GWS score with weaker per-SD OR (1.32 vs 1.42) and smaller validation (n=30,469). PGS000726’s top-vs-bottom OR=2.26 is supportive but doesn’t outweigh the much stronger genome-wide model structure and broader external validation context of PGS004621.

PGS000823 is better supported for the target trait dementia because it comes from a disease-focused Alzheimer’s/dementia cohort study context and reports a PRS effect size (HR 1.36, top vs bottom tertile) on an incident dementia endpoint, giving at least some PRS-specific signal. PGS004281 matches the target label exactly (all-cause dementia) and has large UKB development/validation, but its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC/pseudo-R2 (with age/sex/PCs) and no PGS-only or incremental metric, making the apparent performance largely non-comparable for judging standalone PRS quality. With both lacking clean PRS-only AUC/R2, the presence of a PRS-linked effect size and the more disease-focused multi-cohort archetype favor PGS000823.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to depressive disorder (trait_efo major depressive disorder; phenotyping_reported MDD), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show small full-model/overall R2 ~0.02, which is not strongly comparable). PGS003576 is better supported overall because it has explicit basic covariates (PCs 1–10) and substantially broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/AMR/ASN/EAS/EUR) with multiple performance records (record_count=10), suggesting more transportability evidence than PGS003333, which is EUR-only evaluation with unknown covariates and a single record. While PGS003333 benefits from multi-cohort GWAS sources (23andMe/PGC/UKB) and a stronger shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto), the lack of covariate transparency and narrower validation context make it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS003576.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for dupuytren contracture (same trait_reported, trait_efo, phenotyping_reported), come from the same UKB portability paper, have the same training size, covariates, ancestry distribution, validation size, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r reported). With performance nearly tied (partial-r 0.0797 for PGS002092 vs 0.0783 for PGS001880, overlapping CIs), the main differentiator is structural: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (484,484 vs 2,443), which is generally favored over sparse penalized regression when other evidence is indistinguishable. Hence PGS002092 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS003576 is better supported for depressive disorder because it has tighter endpoint specification (Major Depressive Disorder, lifetime; phenotyping_reported: Major depressive disorder) and substantially richer evaluation context: multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/ASN/EAS/EUR) with a larger validation sample (n=42,250) and explicit training cohort (UKB) with training n=67,164. Although its only reported metric is a full-model R²=0.0241 (not PRS-only), PGS002759 provides even less performance detail (no AUC/R², only a single OR=1.26) and has missing training information (samples_training N/A, no development cohorts listed) and EUR-only evaluation, making its overall evidence package weaker despite using PRS-CS.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to dupuytren contracture (same trait_efo and closely matching phenotyping_reported). PGS001254 has clearly stronger directly comparable PRS-only performance evidence (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646 and PGS-only R² 0.0247 reported), whereas PGS001880 reports only a partial correlation (partial-r 0.0783) and no PRS-comparable AUROC/R², making its predictive strength harder to judge. Although PGS001880 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and a much larger variant set (2443 vs 11), both come from UKB framework/portability-style papers; given that, the presence of explicit PRS-only metrics in PGS001254 is the decisive visible advantage over PGS001880’s less directly interpretable metric package.

PGS000997 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports clean PGS-only AUROC=0.591 and PGS-only R²=0.0178 (no covariates), with basic covariates only (age/sex/PCs/array) and a large, clearly specified UKB training/validation context. PGS004614 is disease-focused and methodologically strong (SBayesR, genome-wide variant count), but its only visible discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.76 with covariates including family history, and it provides no PGS-only AUROC/R² or training sample size—so its apparent performance advantage is likely covariate-driven and not comparable for standalone PRS ranking. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (diverticular disease), so the decisive difference is the availability and cleanliness of PRS-only metrics versus covariate-inflated full-model reporting.

Both candidates target the same trait concept (Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG), EFO dilated cardiomyopathy) with similar PRS-CS construction and EUR-only evaluation, so endpoint alignment is broadly comparable; PGS004951 is slightly more clinically explicit in phenotyping_reported (“Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”) than PGS004862 (“Dilated cardiomyopathy”). Critically, PGS004951 provides a PRS-comparable metric (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI) and PRS delta R² on the liability scale (delta 0.101), whereas PGS004862 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05) that are not directly comparable as PRS-only evidence. PGS004951 also shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.76) and has a larger variant set (1,075,760 vs 709,534), supporting stronger captured polygenic signal. Although PGS004862 has much larger validation N and includes age/sex covariates, validation size is a weak tie-break and the lack of PRS-only metrics limits its support relative to PGS004951’s clearer PRS contribution reporting.

PGS004862 is better supported for the target dilated cardiomyopathy because it is the MTAG-enhanced version of the same disease endpoint (trait_reported: "Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)" vs PGS004861 "Dilated cardiomyopathy"), which domain guidance explicitly notes is mildly preferred as a power-boosting enhancement rather than an endpoint mismatch. Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, PRS-CS, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, identical phenotyping_reported and basic covariates, same validation N), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are weak; still, PGS004862 shows slightly stronger reported full-model AUROC/R² and a higher per-SD OR (1.76 vs 1.56), providing additional supportive evidence over PGS004861.

PGS000997 is better supported for the target trait diverticular disease: it has tighter endpoint fidelity to the EFO-mapped diagnosis ("Diverticular disease of intestine" with explicit TTE phenotyping) whereas PGS000996 mixes endpoints ("diverticular disease/diverticulitis" and trait_efo includes diverticulitis). Both are from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework with identical covariates and ancestry setup, so performance evidence is the main differentiator: PGS000997 shows materially stronger PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.591 vs 0.552; PGS-only R² 0.0178 vs 0.0037) and higher incremental AUROC (0.0173 vs 0.0084). The larger validation N for PGS000996 is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the substantially stronger PRS-only discrimination and cleaner trait focus of PGS000997.

Both candidates target primary open-angle glaucoma, but PGS001792 provides cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a covariates-regressed-out (PGS-only) Nagelkerke R2=0.03209, which is below the glaucoma liability h2 ceiling (~0.0556) and thus plausible. PGS004944 lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2 and only shows a full-model AUROC=0.748, which is not comparable as standalone PRS performance. While PGS004944 reports a strong OR per SD (1.74) and has broad evaluation ancestry, its endpoint is explicitly self-reported POAG and its key metric is full-model only; overall, the explicit PRS-only R2 and clear evaluation context in PGS001792 outweigh PGS004944’s effect-size-only support.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and essentially identical phenotyping_reported). PGS001254 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.6646/0.0247) but comes from a pan-trait sparse snpnet framework with only 11 variants and EUR-only evaluation, a study archetype that domain guidance flags as often less reliable externally. PGS002092, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R², is a genome-wide LDpred2 score with very large variant coverage (484,484) and explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger structural and transportability support for real-world use. Given the framework penalty and extreme sparsity of PGS001254, PGS002092 is better-supported overall despite missing directly comparable AUROC/R².

PGS002304 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000644 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the same EFO, creating endpoint-fidelity ambiguity. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC difference (0.61 for PGS002304 vs 0.538 for PGS000644) is only weakly informative; however, PGS000644’s advantage in method/variant count (lassosum, ~2.2M variants) is not enough to outweigh the clearer phenotype alignment of PGS002304 given the lack of PRS-comparable metrics. Both are EUR-only evaluations; validation size favors PGS000644 but is a weak tie-break, so the decision rests mainly on phenotype fidelity.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same mapped trait (EFO follicular lymphoma) and phenotyping_reported/trait_reported (“Nodular lymphoma”), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI), same training N (3,696), same validation N (3,256), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; the small full-model AUROC difference is likely noise. As a tie-break, PGS000644 has slightly stronger overall discrimination signals (higher full-model AUROC 0.538 vs 0.532; slightly higher per-SD OR 1.149 vs 1.133 and pseudo-R² 0.00349 vs 0.00282), while PGS000643’s higher top-1% OR is less stable given wide CIs. Therefore PGS000644 is marginally better-supported, but confidence is low due to minimal separability.

PGS004951 is better supported for dilated cardiomyopathy because it provides PRS-comparable performance evidence (explicit univariate/PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101), whereas PGS004861 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.70/0.048) without isolating PRS contribution. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both map to dilated cardiomyopathy; PGS004951’s “(MTAG)” is not a mismatch and its phenotyping is explicitly clinical DCM), and covariates are similarly light (sex+PCs vs age/sex/PCs). Although PGS004861 has much larger validation n (347,585 vs 7,761), validation size is a weak tie-breaker and does not outweigh PGS004951’s clearer PRS-only metrics plus stronger reported OR (1.93 vs 1.56).

PGS004614 is the better-supported choice for diverticular disease because it is disease-focused with exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Diverticular disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very large variant coverage (1,082,282), plus multi-ancestry evaluation listed (AFR/EUR/SAS). Although its only visible AUROC (0.76) is a full-model metric and is likely inflated by inclusion of family history (covariates include family history, age, sex), PGS000996’s cleaner PRS-only metrics are very weak (PGS-only AUROC 0.5519; PGS-only R2 0.00372) and it comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse model (368 variants), which domain guidance flags as typically underperforming disease-focused scores. Net: PGS004614 has stronger endpoint fidelity and study archetype/method structure, while PGS000996’s main advantage (explicit PRS-only metrics) indicates only modest PRS signal and is offset by the framework+sparse-model warning.

PGS001792 is better supported for glaucoma PRS quality because it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.03209) with basic covariates (age/sex terms + PCs) and a very large validation sample (n=347,396), while staying endpoint-faithful to glaucoma via a specific POAG phenotype. Its PRS-only R2 is also plausible relative to the glaucoma liability h2 ceiling (~0.0556). In contrast, PGS000137 has no PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC=0.8) and its covariates include self-reported family history, which can inflate full-model discrimination and makes the reported AUROC less informative for standalone PRS comparison; it also has much smaller training/validation samples (training n=8,004; validation n=1,795).

PGS002304 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000643 is labeled “Nodular lymphoma” (despite mapping to the same EFO), introducing phenotype/label ambiguity. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS002304 shows higher AUROC (0.61 vs 0.532) without evidence of heavy covariate packaging (covariates unknown vs PGS000643’s age/sex/PCs). Although PGS000643 has a stronger genome-wide method/variant count (PRS-CS; ~1.0M variants) and larger validation n, the combination of exact phenotype fidelity and better observed discrimination favors PGS002304 overall.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), study context (same publication, UKB training n=6,704), covariates (0), ancestry distribution (DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS), and validation size (n=90,274). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers. On the visible metrics, PGS004160 is consistently slightly stronger than PGS004047 (full-model AUROC 0.6936 vs 0.6851; R² 0.0893 vs 0.0801; OR per SD 2.05 vs 2.00), and it also has a higher variant count (976,174 vs 865,644) plus an ensemble-style method label (MultiPRS) versus a single-method LDpred2. Given otherwise identical design, these small but consistent advantages favor PGS004160.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS001789 provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2 / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 = 0.0312) with basic demographic/PC covariates and broad multi-cohort, multi-ancestry development plus large validation (n=359,345), giving more directly interpretable PRS evidence and better transportability context. PGS004047 lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R2 are shown), making its performance less comparable for PRS ranking despite reporting strong per-SD OR≈2.0; it is also developed only in UKB with smaller training (n=6,704) and narrower development ancestry. Heritability ceiling sanity-check is feasible for PGS001789’s PRS R2 (below h2_liability≈0.0525), further supporting metric plausibility.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, and have identical evaluation ancestry and validation sample size (MAE 100%, n=94,651), with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported—so full-model AUROC differences (0.639 for PGS005270 vs 0.605 for PGS005272) are not decisive. Under the fallback guidance when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS005272 is better supported structurally and by PRS signal: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with far more variants (1,085,142 vs 55) and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.42 vs 1.04), indicating materially stronger discriminative power than the sparse P+T score PGS005270.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (trait_efo) with identical reported/phenotyped endpoint (“lymphocytic thyroiditis”), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%), same validation size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, which is not a reliable differentiator). In this near-clone setting, PGS005271 has materially stronger PRS signal evidence via effect size (OR per SD 1.55 vs 1.04 for PGS005270) and a structurally stronger genome-wide shrinkage approach with far broader variant coverage (PRS-CS, ~1.09M variants vs P+T, 55 variants), which is the more reliable tie-break than the small full-model AUROC difference (0.630 vs 0.639).

PGS002763 is the better-supported hip osteoarthritis PRS on endpoint fidelity and comparability: it directly targets “Hip osteoarthritis” with matching phenotyping_reported, and it reports a clearer, stronger PRS effect size (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.31–1.46) with basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), reducing risk of hidden clinical packaging. PGS004478 maps to the same EFO but uses an ICD-style label (“M16 Coxarthrosis”) with unknown covariates and comes from a risk-factor integration framing, which raises concern about non-genetic augmentation even though no AUC/R2 is shown; its reported OR (~1.30, no CI) is also weaker. With neither candidate providing PRS-only AUC/R2, the stronger endpoint clarity + effect-size evidence favors PGS002763.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS001789 provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.031208) with basic demographic/PC covariates and very broad multi-biobank development plus large validation (n=359,345) and multi-ancestry GWAS/eval context, supporting transportability. In contrast, PGS004160 reports only full-model metrics (AUROC and R²) with no PGS-only AUC/R², making its performance less directly attributable to the PRS; it is also developed only in UKB EUR with a much smaller training sample (n=6,704) and narrower validation (EUR/SAS; n=90,274). Given the heritability ceiling guidance, PGS001789’s PRS-only R² is interpretable and below the gout h2_liability estimate, whereas PGS004160’s reported R² is not clearly PRS-only. Overall evidence favors PGS001789.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication, have identical EUR-only ancestry context, identical training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so we must rely on the available full-model metrics and effect sizes as supportive evidence. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger validation signals than PGS000637: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), and stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.476 vs 1.3). Although PGS000637 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with many variants, within this same-endpoint sibling comparison the empirical performance/effect-size evidence favors PGS000639.

PGS004944 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint is tightly aligned to glaucoma via a specific dominant subtype (trait_reported: primary open-angle glaucoma; trait_efo: open-angle glaucoma; phenotyping: self-reported POAG) and it shows PRS signal via an effect size (OR per SD 1.74, strong) with only basic covariates (age/age^2/sex/ancestry), reducing covariate-leakage concerns. It also uses a genome-wide shrinkage-style approach (Lassosum) with very large variant coverage (144,019) and is evaluated at large scale (n=407,667) across multiple ancestries, supporting transportability. In contrast, PGS000137 has broader/less specific trait labeling (trait_reported glaucoma but phenotyping POAG) and its reported AUROC=0.8 is a full-model metric with inclusion of family history as a covariate, making the discrimination less comparable to PRS-only performance; it also uses a sparse C+T score with far fewer variants (2,673) and smaller validation (n=1,795). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so structural signals and covariate cleanliness favor PGS004944.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication/cohort context (MGI; EUR-only; same training n=736 and validation n=775), and use similarly clean basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so full-model AUROC is only a secondary within-family comparator. On the visible evaluation record, PGS000638 shows consistently stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000637: higher full-model AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.013), plus a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). While PGS000637 uses a genome-wide PRS-CS model with many more variants, within this same-endpoint sibling comparison the observed discrimination/effect-size evidence favors PGS000638, and the AUROC gap (~0.03) aligns with that direction.

PGS002728 is better supported for the target hip osteoarthritis because its endpoint is clinically anchored (phenotyping_reported: total hip replacement) and it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort osteoarthritis PRS study with explicit basic covariates (age, sex) and a reported AUROC (0.66, albeit full-model). In contrast, PGS004478 is a lone ICD-style code model (M16 coxarthrosis) from a broader “risk factor PRS + disease PRS integration” framework with unknown covariates and no discrimination metrics (no AUROC/R2; only a modest per-SD OR≈1.30), making its PRS evidence and comparability weaker despite larger training/validation sizes and a genome-wide LDpred2 construction.

PGS001790 is the better-supported heart failure PRS because it provides a clean PRS-comparable performance metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.006981) with basic covariates and a very large EUR validation sample (n=358,905), and its endpoint fields are directly aligned (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all heart failure). PGS005083 has a reasonably aligned but narrower phecode endpoint (CHF NOS) and reports only full-model discrimination (C-index ~0.754) plus an OR=1.455, but lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive evidence less directly comparable; its smaller validation size (n=31,804) and single-cohort development (MVP) do not compensate for the missing PRS-only metric. Both use only basic covariates, so covariate leakage is not a differentiator.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo = heart failure), but PGS005097 comes from a disease-focused heart-failure genetics study (Nat Genet: "genetic architecture of heart failure") with basic covariates (age, sex, 5 PCs) and uses PRS-CSx with broader GWAS ancestry inputs and a multi-ancestry evaluation context (European + African unspecified), which is supportive for transportability. PGS001790 is from a known portability/framework-style paper ("Global Biobank analyses provide lessons...") and, while it reports a PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 covariates-regressed-out = 0.006981, below the heritability ceiling), its evaluation is EUR-only and its apparent AUROC advantage is full-model (not PRS-only) with heavier covariate terms. Given the framework penalty and stronger disease-focused endpoint/study archetype for PGS005097, it is better-supported overall despite lacking explicit PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI), same training n=736 and validation n=775, and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so endpoint fidelity and transportability do not differentiate. PGS000639 is better supported on the available performance/effect-size evidence: slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601) and Nagelkerke R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.476 vs 1.377; β 0.39 vs 0.32). Given the same study context, these consistent advantages outweigh the small method/variant-count differences, so PGS000639 is the stronger pick.

PGS005097 is the better-supported match to the target trait (heart failure): its trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported (“Prevalent heart failure”) directly align with the generic heart failure endpoint, whereas PGS005083 targets a narrower/administrative EHR definition (“CHF, NOS (PheCode 428.1)”) and maps to “congestive heart failure,” which is close but less faithful to the broad target. Study archetype and transportability also favor PGS005097: it is developed in a disease-focused multi-cohort setting (many HF-relevant biobanks/consortia listed) with a cross-ancestry GWAS base, while PGS005083 comes from a methods-comparison/portability-style paper with development limited to MVP. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2; both report only full-model discrimination (AUC/C-index) with basic covariates, so PGS005083’s slightly higher full-model C-index and OR=1.455 are not enough to outweigh PGS005097’s stronger endpoint fidelity and broader, disease-focused multi-cohort support.

PGS002763 has higher endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is directly “Hip osteoarthritis,” matching the target, whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a proxy/treatment endpoint that can reflect access/surgical decision and disease severity rather than hip OA status. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002728’s full-model AUROC=0.66 (age, sex) is not a comparable PRS metric and shouldn’t outweigh endpoint mismatch. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants and provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.38), while PGS002728 is a sparse 44-variant GWS score with no effect-size evidence shown. Both are EUR-only evaluation; validation N is larger for PGS002763 (39,444 vs 14,926), but this is secondary to the stronger endpoint alignment and more polygenic model structure.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis; same method PRSCS; same evaluation ancestry mix and validation n=94,651; covariates unknown; no PRS-only AUC/R2). With endpoint fidelity and study context essentially identical, the differentiators are the available performance/effect-size signals: PGS005271 shows higher reported AUROC in the selected record (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.55 vs 1.42; β 0.438 vs 0.349). Training-cohort breadth is slightly larger for PGS005271 (includes BBJ, MVP) but is a weak tie-break. Overall, PGS005271 has the stronger empirical signal while PGS005272 lacks any compensating advantage.

Both candidates target hypertension, but PGS004236 is from a disease-focused multi-ethnic hypertension study (Nat Commun) with multi-cohort development (BioMe, MVP, UKB) and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1 per SD), supporting meaningful genetic discrimination even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided. PGS001320 has clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649) and large UKB training/validation, but it comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization despite well-formatted metrics. Given the stronger disease-focused archetype and effect-size evidence for PGS004236 versus the framework-origin penalty for PGS001320, PGS004236 is better-supported overall, though confidence is tempered by PGS004236’s lack of PRS-only AUC/R2 and its covariate-heavier reported AUROC being full-model.

PGS001320 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence for hypertension: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R2=0.06493 (no-covariates), enabling direct PRS assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check, whereas PGS004234 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.763 with no PGS-only metrics, so its discrimination is not comparable and may be covariate-driven (it includes BMI, smoking, race/ethnic background, site, etc.). Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both, but PGS004234’s phenotyping is explicitly “Prevelant hypertension” (minor mismatch/typo) while PGS001320 is a direct “Hypertension” phenotype. Although PGS004234 is from a disease-focused multi-ethnic study with diverse evaluation ancestries, the lack of PRS-only metrics and heavier covariate set makes its support weaker on the visible fields than PGS001320’s directly comparable PRS-only validation.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo = hypertension; phenotyping_reported = prevalent hypertension), come from the same publication, have the same training N (10,314), similar covariates (age/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), and identical validation sample size (39,035) with MAE evaluation—so full-model AUROC 0.764 vs 0.763 is essentially noise and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS004236 is better supported because it provides additional PRS-relevant evidence (effect size OR=2.1 per SD with CI) that PGS004234 lacks, and it is structurally more genome-wide (398,805 vs 234,228 variants) with a multi-score aggregation-style method label (PRSsum) versus a single C+T pipeline (PRSice-2), which is a mild advantage when other fields are near-identical.

Both candidates are near-clones for the hyperthyroidism target via the clinically dominant subtype Graves’ disease (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix, and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With endpoints and study context effectively identical, the best available differentiators are effect-size strength and small full-model AUROC differences: PGS005265 shows slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and a stronger per-SD OR (1.625 vs 1.543) than PGS005266, while variant counts are essentially the same. Therefore PGS005265 is better supported on the visible evidence, though confidence is only moderate because the records are extremely similar and lack PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet study with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported both hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), identical covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same development cohorts, and same validation sample size; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak differentiator. Given that, PGS004911 has consistently stronger visible performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (higher full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; higher R² 0.048 vs 0.031; higher HR 2.34 vs 1.97; slightly higher OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; slightly higher high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced version, which domain guidance treats as a legitimate power-boost and mildly preferred over the non-MTAG sibling when other fields are comparable.

PGS004911 is better supported as a standalone PRS for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (374,114) and reports PRS-linked effect sizes (OR per SD 1.33; HR 2.34; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), reducing concern that performance is driven by clinical packaging. PGS000739, while endpoint-aligned, is a sparse 27-variant GWAS-hits score and its reported AUROC (0.821) comes from a model explicitly adjusted for multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status, making the full-model AUROC less informative about PRS contribution (and no PGS-only metrics are provided). With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, the cleaner covariate context and stronger polygenic construction favor PGS004911.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all the generic JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly restricted to the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a broad JIA target). Both are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same basic covariates (sex, PCs), and EUR-only dev/eval, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not decisive). Although PGS000325 shows higher full-model AUROC and larger validation N, those are weak tie-breakers and don’t outweigh the broader endpoint fidelity of PGS000114 for the generic JIA target.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Disorders of iron metabolism”), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and identical multi-ancestry evaluation distribution/validation N (n=19,883). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are structural and the available PRS-comparable metric: PGS002031 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with many more variants (6,713 vs 654) and shows slightly higher partial correlation (0.1355 vs 0.1307). Given the same endpoint and evaluation context, the higher-coverage shrinkage model with marginally better partial-r is better supported than the sparser penalized-regression score (PGS001823).

PGS005218 is better supported overall: it is from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with a much broader multi-cohort development set (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,110,091), whereas PGS004935 comes from a portability/framework-style paper (single UKB development) using a sparse SnpNet score (6,127 variants), which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external generalization. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so neither full-model AUROC is directly comparable; moreover PGS005218’s high AUROC (0.859) is explicitly biomarker-augmented (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making it non-informative for PRS strength, but PGS004935’s AUROC (0.7) is also only full-model with unknown covariates. With comparable trait alignment (both hypothyroidism) and no clean PRS-only metrics, the stronger study archetype and structural properties favor PGS005218 despite the covariate-heavy evaluation.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are EUR-trained/evaluated in UKB, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported. PGS004935’s only discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC=0.7 with unknown covariates, which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven; its OR per SD is 1.5 but with smaller validation (n=8,417) and a sparse-ish 6,127-variant SnpNet score from a portability-style paper. PGS002766 provides a cleaner disclosed covariate set (age, sex, PCs, technical), a much larger genome-wide PRS-CS model (1,092,122 variants; structurally better for polygenic signal capture), and a very similar OR (1.47) with substantially larger validation (n=39,444). With comparable endpoint fidelity and no PRS-only metrics to separate them, the stronger method/variant coverage plus clearer evaluation setup favors PGS002766.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint fidelity is an exact match at all key fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different trait_efo and phenotyping_reported, making it less directly aligned to the broad target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so metrics are not cleanly comparable; in that setting, PGS000114 also has stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51 for PGS000326) and a larger variant set (26 vs 12) with otherwise similar covariates (sex, PCs) and identical study family/ancestry context. PGS000326’s slightly higher full-model AUROC and larger validation N are weak tie-breakers and don’t outweigh the broader endpoint match and stronger OR for PGS000114.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar EUR-only DEV/EVAL ancestry, identical basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is discounted). Given this near-clone context, PGS000325 has stronger visible performance evidence: higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.76) and a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.51), plus slightly more variants (21 vs 12). Endpoint-wise both are JIA subtypes; neither is the generic JIA umbrella, so fidelity is comparable. Therefore PGS000325 is better supported than PGS000326 on the available fields.

PGS005266 is better supported for the target trait hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease) is the clinically dominant autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism and is explicitly noted as a strong match for a generic hyperthyroidism target, whereas PGS001043 is a pan-trait UK Biobank “813 traits” sparse framework score that domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable in external validation. Although PGS001043 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6323; PGS R² 0.02158, below the h2 ceiling and thus plausible) with basic covariates, its study archetype and very sparse 69-variant model are weaker structural/transportability signals than PGS005266’s disease-focused multi-cohort development across many biobanks and genome-wide PRS-CS construction (1,085,170 variants) with large multi-ancestry evaluation (n=94,651). PGS005266 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC shown), which lowers certainty, but the combination of dominant-subtype fidelity plus disease-focused multi-biobank context outweighs the framework-score metric advantage here.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) with a much larger, richer variant set (107 vs 19) and a substantially stronger PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.5 vs PGS000076 HR 1.16), suggesting meaningfully higher standalone genetic discrimination even though neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2. Both candidates only provide full-model AUROC (0.74 for PGS004908 vs 0.722 for PGS000076), which is not PRS-comparable and both use similar epidemiologic covariates, so the small AUROC difference is weak evidence; the stronger effect size and more disease-focused development context favor PGS004908. PGS000076 has a slightly larger validation N and an incident endpoint plus RCC mapping (a good match), but it appears as a cross-cancer evaluation with weaker per-SD risk signal and a much sparser score, so it loses overall.

PGS004562 is the better-supported kidney failure candidate because its endpoint is a direct diagnosis-code phenotype (N18 chronic renal failure) aligned to kidney failure, whereas PGS000708’s phenotyping is explicitly restricted to “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a narrower subtype that is less faithful to the generic target trait. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparability relies on effect sizes: PGS004562 shows a moderate OR=1.395 per SD, while PGS000708 shows a weaker HR=1.19 per SD and only a full-model C-index (0.779) that is not PRS-comparable. Although PGS000708 has clearer covariates and larger validation, PGS004562’s stronger PRS effect size and broader phenotype match outweigh the missing covariate detail.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS000739’s higher full-model AUROC (0.821 vs 0.73) is heavily discounted because its covariates include substantial clinical packaging (obesity, HTN, AF, CAD) plus rare-variant carrier status, making the metric likely covariate-driven and less informative about the PRS itself. PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that leakage concern, and provides supportive PRS signal via effect sizes (e.g., HR 1.97; OR high vs median tertile 5.5) alongside a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant count (374,190 vs 27), which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic architecture. Overall, PGS004910 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for HCM, despite PGS000739’s larger reported full-model AUROC.

PGS005218 is better supported on study design and endpoint specificity: it comes from a hypothyroidism-focused GWAS/prediction paper with very large multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and a large European evaluation (n=441,692) with an explicitly incident hypothyroidism endpoint. PGS002766 is from a cross-disease family-history vs PRS comparison framework in UKB only, with no training sample reported and only a single validation record; while it reports a solid PRS effect size (OR=1.47 per SD), it lacks broader development/validation context. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, and PGS005218’s reported AUROC is full-model and covariate-heavy (includes TSH/T4/anti-TPO), so metrics don’t drive the decision; the win is primarily due to stronger disease-focused multi-cohort evidence and clearer endpoint definition versus the more framework-like UKB-only comparator.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it is a disease-focused kidney-cancer GWAS meta-analysis score (Nat Genet; multi-ancestry discovery) with a much stronger PRS effect size signal (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) and a substantially richer variant set (107 GWAS-significant SNPs) than PGS000787 (19 variants; HR 1.15, 1.07–1.24). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R², so their similar full-model AUROC values (0.74 vs 0.722) are not decisive and are further confounded by non-genetic covariates in both. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (PGS004908 ‘Kidney cancer’; PGS000787 ‘Incident kidney cancer’ and RCC is a dominant subtype), but PGS000787 comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration framework and is explicitly built by reweighting another score, which is weaker direct evidence than the dedicated kidney-cancer susceptibility-region study underlying PGS004908.

PGS002767 is the better-supported standalone PRS for knee osteoarthritis: it has exact endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported = "Knee osteoarthritis") and provides a PRS-specific effect size (OR per SD 1.35, moderate signal) with only basic demographic/PC/technical covariates, consistent with a cleaner PRS evaluation. PGS002729, while disease-focused and listing many development cohorts, reports only a full-model AUROC (0.66) with covariates including BMI and has a less specific endpoint label (phenotyping_reported = "Clinical osteoarthritis"), and full-model AUROC is not PRS-comparable when PGS-only metrics are absent. With both lacking PGS-only AUC/R2, the combination of tighter phenotype match plus genome-wide shrinkage construction (PRS-CS, 1,052,275 variants) makes PGS002767 the stronger choice over the sparse 24-variant GWAS-hits score.

PGS000708 is better supported on the visible fields for the target trait kidney failure: it has direct trait_reported alignment (“Kidney failure”) and provides more interpretable evaluation evidence (a reported C-index/full-model 0.779 plus an HR=1.19 with CI) with clearly stated basic covariates (age as time scale, sex, batch, PCs), which reduces comparability concerns. PGS004492 maps to the same EFO via an ICD-10-style endpoint (N18 chronic renal failure) but has weaker metadata support: covariates are unknown, performance metrics are essentially absent (no AUC/R2/C-index), and only a modest OR≈1.17 is given without CI. Although PGS004492 uses LDpred2 with many more variants, the lack of comparable performance/covariate detail makes it less well-supported overall than PGS000708.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (N18 chronic renal failure) mapped to kidney failure, same publication, same EUR-only development/evaluation, same training cohort (UKB), same training N and validation N, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so metrics can’t differentiate cleanly). The main differentiator is the available PRS signal via effect size: PGS004562 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.395) than PGS004492 (1.171), suggesting better standalone discriminative power given otherwise matched design. Method differences (metaPRS vs LDpred2) are secondary here because there’s no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 to show LDpred2 actually performs better in this setting.

PGS005265 is better supported for the target trait (hyperthyroidism) because its endpoint is Graves’ disease, which is a clinically dominant autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a large multi-cohort, multi-biobank study context with broad external evaluation (validation n=94,651; evaluation in MAE with selected validation ancestries including African American/Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, and European). It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.63), which is meaningful PRS signal even though only a full-model AUROC is shown (0.665) and PRS-only AUC/R2 are missing. In contrast, PGS001043 is an exact-label hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis score with clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.6323; R2=0.0216, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-framework paper (“across 813 traits”) with a very small variant set (69) and single-biobank development, which is a known weaker archetype for external generalization versus disease-focused multi-cohort models. Overall, the disease-focused multi-cohort design plus strong OR and dominant-subtype alignment outweigh the framework score’s advantage of having PRS-only AUROC/R2.

PGS002729 is a direct, disease-focused knee osteoarthritis PRS with clear clinical endpoint labeling (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both knee/clinical osteoarthritis) and transparent basic covariates (age, sex, BMI). It also provides at least a reported discrimination figure (AUROC 0.66) albeit as a full-model metric, giving some performance context. In contrast, PGS004549 comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with an ICD-style label (M17 gonarthrosis), unknown covariates, and no AUC/R2 reported—only a modest per-SD OR (~1.37). Despite PGS004549’s much larger genome-wide variant count and larger training/validation N, the lack of comparable PRS performance metrics and the risk-factor integration framing make it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS002729 for knee osteoarthritis.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), identical ancestry context (EUR GWAS/EVAL), identical covariates, identical variant count (19), and essentially identical full-model discrimination/effect sizes (AUROC 0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724; HR per SD ~1.15–1.16). However, PGS000787 is explicitly a derivative/packaging of PGS000076 (“19 variants from Graff et al (PGS000076) with inverse variant weights”), offering no independent training or clearer PRS-only performance evidence (both lack PGS-only AUC/R2). Its additional reported R²=0.366 appears to be a full-model/other metric and is not PRS-comparable, and is also implausibly above the provided kidney-cancer heritability ceiling for PRS-only interpretation, so it cannot justify selecting the derivative. Therefore the original, directly specified score PGS000076 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS002767 is the better-supported standalone PRS for the target knee osteoarthritis endpoint: it has direct phenotype fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Knee osteoarthritis”) and transparent basic covariate adjustment (age, sex, PCs, technical covariates), with a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.35, 95% CI 1.3–1.4) in EUR evaluation. PGS004549 maps to the same EFO but is explicitly an integrated risk-factor + disease metaPRS (“Integration of risk factor polygenic risk score with disease polygenic risk score”), which is a packaging/augmentation signal for standalone PRS comparability, and its covariates are unknown—making its reported OR (1.3667) harder to interpret as PRS-only evidence. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either model, endpoint fidelity and avoidance of risk-factor integration favor PGS002767 despite PGS004549’s larger training/validation sizes.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease), same phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (genome-wide significant variants) and variant count (21), same basic covariates (age, sex), same publication/date, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2. With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available effect size: PGS000054 reports a materially stronger OR per SD (1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR 1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is stronger evidence of PRS discriminative signal. PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-on-EUR evaluation, but validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger OR evidence in PGS000054.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. However, PGS000789 is explicitly a pan-cancer risk-prediction package that integrates many non-genetic factors including family history, detailed smoking variables with interaction terms, and PM2.5—heavy covariate augmentation that makes its high full-model AUROC/R² largely non-informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS004860 is from a lung-cancer-focused study and uses a genome-wide LDpred2 score (1,143,554 variants) with a comparatively lighter covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking status/PCs), and it shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.33 vs HR 1.17), supporting a stronger PRS signal despite the smaller validation sample.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo are lung cancer/lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported is incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS and EUR evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable PRS metrics. Given that, PGS004860 has stronger structural support for capturing polygenic signal (LDpred2 with 1,143,554 variants vs PGS000078 genome-wide significant hits with 109 variants) and a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.33 vs HR=1.16), suggesting better standalone PRS discrimination. PGS000078 also has heavier covariate packaging (family history, PM2.5, detailed smoking variables and interactions), making its full-model AUROC (0.846) more covariate-driven and less informative about PRS contribution than PGS004860’s simpler covariate set. Although PGS000078 has much larger validation n, validation size is a weak tie-breaker and doesn’t outweigh the method/variant-count and effect-size advantages for PGS004860.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo is late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so performance comparability relies on secondary evidence. PGS000053 provides a PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.29, moderate signal) and has clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex), reducing concern about covariate-driven inflation. PGS000334 reports only a full-model/unspecified R²=0.191 with unknown covariates, which is not PRS-comparable and is also suspiciously high relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0084; h2_liability≈0.0269), suggesting non-comparable scaling or covariate/packaging influence. With cleaner covariate disclosure and a direct PRS effect size, PGS000053 is better-supported on the visible fields despite similar validation sizes and EUR evaluation.

PGS000788 is better supported for the target trait despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, because it has stronger endpoint fidelity and a more credible evidence package than PGS000645. Both map to the same EFO (lymphoid leukemia), but PGS000788’s phenotyping is explicitly an incident lymphocytic leukemia endpoint and it reports a strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.7), whereas PGS000645 is a very sparse 6-variant P+T score with only moderate per-SD association (OR=1.358) and weak full-model discrimination (AUROC=0.578). Neither candidate provides PRS-only metrics, so full-model AUROC is not a reliable differentiator; in that setting, PGS000788’s substantially larger variant set (75 vs 6) and stronger effect-size evidence outweigh PGS000645’s cleaner single-cohort EUR-only development metadata.

PGS000754 is the better match to the target trait (lupus erythematosus) because its phenotyping_reported is the general systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosis, whereas PGS000328 is explicitly restricted to early-onset SLE (onset before age 20), a subtype/age-conditioned endpoint that is less faithful for generic lupus risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so the higher AUROC for PGS000328 (0.83 vs 0.65) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage and could reflect covariate/modeling differences (covariates unknown for both). With metrics essentially non-comparable, structural signals favor PGS000754’s genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with far more variants (293,684 vs 57), which is generally more appropriate for a polygenic disease endpoint than a small GWAS-hit score, especially when the latter is also endpoint-restricted.

PGS000328 is better aligned to the target trait as a direct systemic lupus erythematosus score evaluated in a clear SLE-focused context (early-onset SLE), whereas PGS000196’s phenotyping is framed as “SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis,” which is a more context-restricted outpatient differential-diagnosis setting. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.83 for PGS000328 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) are only weakly informative; still, PGS000328 is at least not worse on the visible discrimination. Ancestry-wise, both are EUR-trained; PGS000196 has some non-EUR evaluation (MAE 33%), but given the endpoint/context mismatch and lack of PRS-only metrics, that does not outweigh PGS000328’s cleaner endpoint fidelity and slightly stronger reported AUROC.

Both candidates are essentially the same lung cancer endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported = incident lung cancer), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariate bundle (including smoking variables, PM2.5, and family history), and nearly identical reported full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) and HR per SD (~1.16–1.17). Candidate_b (PGS000789) is explicitly derived from candidate_a (PGS000078) by inverting weights, and its additional R²=0.799 appears to be a full-model/other metric (not PRS-only) and is also implausibly high relative to the lung cancer heritability ceiling provided, making it non-comparable and not a reliable advantage. With no PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the base, directly constructed GWAS-hits score (PGS000078) is marginally better-supported than an inverse-weight derivative (PGS000789).

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia; phenotyping_reported=Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia) and use similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) with the same EUR evaluation ancestry and identical validation sample size (n=391,338). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS000788 shows consistently stronger available performance signals than PGS000077 (higher AUROC 0.738 vs 0.719, higher C-index 0.756 vs 0.735, and stronger HR per SD 1.70 vs 1.45). Methodologically, PGS000788 is a reweighted derivative of PGS000077, and the observed stronger effect-size/discrimination evidence in the same endpoint/validation context supports selecting PGS000788.

Both candidates target systemic lupus erythematosus (trait_reported/efo match), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). Candidate_a (PGS000754) has higher endpoint fidelity in phenotyping_reported (straight “Systemic lupus erythematosus”) and comes from a disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis context with a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) and very large variant count (293,684), which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic autoimmune disease than candidate_b’s very sparse P+T score (55 variants). Candidate_b (PGS000196) shows a higher full-model AUROC (0.79 vs 0.65) but it is not interpretable as PRS strength and is paired with a more context-specific outpatient/arthritis diagnostic framing (“SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis”) plus a much smaller validation sample (n=245 vs n=7,733). Overall, PGS000754 is better-supported on phenotype fidelity and model structure; confidence is moderate because both lack PRS-only metrics and covariates are unknown.

Both candidates match the target trait well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease in trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported). Neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R², so performance must be judged via other visible evidence. PGS000054 has stronger PRS-discrimination support via an explicit per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) and clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex), plus a broad multi-cohort disease-focused development set (many AD cohorts/consortia) and external evaluation in AMR (Hispanic/Latin American), which is informative for transportability. Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (melanoma), same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication and validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not strong cross-model PRS comparators). Both candidates are near-clones for the target myocardial infarction endpoint (same PheCode 411.2, same trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported), from the same publication, with identical covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), training cohort (MVP), ancestry distribution, and validation sample size (n=30,379). Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), identical ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002306 (0.69 vs 0.577) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage. Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align; EUR GWAS and EUR evaluation). Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (benign nodular goiter), same phenotyping string (typoed but matching), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported. The cohort list is marginally broader for PGS005262 (includes BBJ and CKB), but this is a weak signal. Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis). However, PGS002038 comes from a UKB “portability of 245 scores” framework paper and reports only a weak PRS-comparable metric (partial-r=0.0396) with no AUROC/R²/effect-size discrimination, making its disease-specific support and PRS strength harder to trust despite larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation. Given the framework-penalty and weak metric evidence for PGS002038, the better-supported MS-specific candidate is PGS000809.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS002726 is from a disease-focused MS susceptibility/phenotype paper (IMSGC-based) and provides stronger disease-relevant performance evidence via a reported AUROC 0.80 (though it is a full-model metric, not PRS-only) plus a very large risk stratification effect (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0). In contrast, PGS002038 comes from a UKB portability framework study ("Portability of 245 polygenic scores"), which is penalized as a pan-trait/framework archetype, and its only visible performance signal is a modest partial correlation (partial-r = 0.0396) without any AUROC/PRS-only metric. Despite PGS002038 having larger training and multi-ancestry evaluation, the framework context and weaker effect-size evidence make PGS002726 better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS002247 is better supported for the target melanoma endpoint because its phenotyping is more deployment-faithful and less clinically packaged: it targets "Incident invasive melanoma" with only basic covariates (age, sex), whereas PGS000743 reports performance in a model heavily adjusted for traditional melanoma risk factors including family history and personal history of keratinocyte cancer, making its full-model AUROC (0.74) largely non-comparable to PRS quality. With endpoints aligned (both melanoma, EUR eval), PGS002247’s cleaner covariate context and larger variant set (68 vs 45) outweigh PGS000743’s covariate-inflated AUROC.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to the target (trait_efo = nicotine dependence; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported = Tobacco use disorder), come from the same UKB portability paper, have identical training size (n=391,124), similar multi-ancestry evaluation, identical covariates, and the same validation sample size (n=19,400), so the decision rests on PRS-comparable performance and structural method signals. PGS001830’s sparse penalized regression and lower partial-r provide weaker support in this near-clone comparison.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported ICD10 J33; trait_efo Nasal Cavity Polyp), come from the same publication, and have the same EUR-only UKB training (n=174,489), EUR-only evaluation, identical variant count (1,059,939), and identical validation size (n=56,192), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so metrics and transportability do not differentiate. Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; same phenotyping_reported string) and come from the same multi-biobank study with identical ancestry_distribution, cohorts, and validation_sample_size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS metric). Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from spelling), come from the same publication family, and have the same evaluation ancestry and validation sample size (n=94,651), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so full-model AUROC differences (0.5876 in PGS005263 vs 0.5854 in PGS005261) are essentially non-decisive. Both candidates target the same endpoint with identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, come from the same UKB portability paper, use the same training cohort (UKB), same training size (n=391,124), same covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), and have the same multi-ancestry evaluation distribution and validation sample size (n=19,668). Neither reports clean PGS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint specificity + effect-size evidence + disease-focused design favor PGS005217.

It also comes from a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort Nat Med study with explicit training/development cohorts listed and a defined training sample size (n=212,034), which is stronger study-context evidence than PGS004593’s missing training sample and empty development-cohort list. Both candidates lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so effect-size evidence is used; both show similar moderate per-SD effects (OR 1.20 for PGS003587 vs HR 1.16 for PGS004593), not enough to outweigh the study-design and endpoint-coherence advantage of PGS003587. PGS004593 has an exact trait_reported label but its phenotyping_reported is gestational hypertension (a partial mismatch for preeclampsia), making its endpoint fidelity weaker despite larger validation N.

PGS003586 is the better-supported match for the target trait preeclampsia because its trait_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia” with the same trait_efo (preeclampsia) and the same phenotyping_reported (“Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia”) as candidate_b, so endpoint fidelity favors candidate_a on the visible label alignment. Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, method PRS-CS, similar ~1.09M variants, same EUR-only development/evaluation, same covariates, same training n and validation n, and no PRS-only AUC/R2). The full-model C-index in PGS005217 is not treated as PRS-only, but the combination of disease-focused design plus strong HR and broader external evaluation makes it the stronger candidate overall.

Although PGS002083 has more variants and larger training N, those are weaker signals than having clean PRS-only metrics; thus PGS001312 is the stronger, better-evidenced record here.

PGS001312 is the better-supported match to the generic target trait psoriasis: it uses a direct psoriasis phenotype (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Psoriasis”), whereas PGS001313 is explicitly time-to-event (“Psoriasis (time-to-event)”, phenotyping_reported “TTE psoriasis”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for generic disease status. Both are otherwise near-clones (same pan-trait UKB framework paper, same snpnet method family, same EUR-only development and identical multi-ancestry evaluation mix, same covariates, same training and validation sizes). With endpoints acceptable, PGS001312 also has slightly stronger PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.6916 vs 0.6729; PGS-only R² 0.0523 vs 0.0497; incremental AUROC 0.1451 vs 0.1385), so it wins on both fidelity and metrics.

PGS001280 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.60765) and PGS-only R² (0.01403) with basic covariates listed, enabling a clean PRS contribution readout and a heritability-ceiling sanity check. PGS003861 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.765) with covariates unknown and no PGS-only AUC/R², so its discrimination is not comparable and could be largely covariate-driven; its OR metric is also quantile-based and not directly comparable to PRS-per-SD. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (pulmonary embolism), but PGS001280 additionally has broader multi-ancestry evaluation (incl. AFR/EAS/SAS) versus PGS003861 being EAS-only, improving robustness evidence despite PGS001280’s pan-trait UKB framework origin.

PGS001287 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (AUROC=0.67648; R²=0.0335) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array) and large-scale UKB development (n=269,704) plus a clearly specified European validation record (n=24,905). Its PGS-only R² is also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (well below h2_liability=0.0735). In contrast, PGS000342 is disease-focused and endpoint-faithful (Psoriatic arthritis) but provides only a full-model AUROC=0.562 with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its predictive support and comparability much weaker. While PGS001287 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a negative archetype signal), the substantial, clean PRS-only performance evidence and larger, clearer validation context outweigh PGS000342’s sparse 11-variant score with limited metric transparency.

PGS001313 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and endpoint documentation: it reports explicit PRS-only AUROC (0.6729 with CI) and PRS-only R² (0.04966) under basic covariates, whereas PGS002083 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0632) and no AUROC/R², making cross-model PRS discrimination harder to assess. Both map cleanly to psoriasis (trait_efo=psoriasis), but PGS001313’s phenotyping is clearly specified (time-to-event psoriasis) and it also has a larger, more diverse evaluation set (n=67,425 across AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) than PGS002083 (n=19,615; includes GME but smaller overall). Although both are UKB framework-style scores (813-traits sparse vs portability sweep), the stronger directly comparable PRS-only metrics and broader validation evidence favor PGS001313.

PGS001791 is better supported for pulmonary fibrosis/IPF because it provides a clean PRS-comparable performance metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.005929) in a large EUR evaluation (n=347,350) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, and the R2 is plausible relative to the trait’s low observed-scale heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0039) as a sanity check. In contrast, PGS004695 is an incident-IPF time-to-event framing from an exposure-focused study and reports no PRS-only AUC/R2 at all—only an HR (high vs low quintile)=3.78 that is less directly comparable and is conditioned on a broader epidemiologic covariate set (education, smoking, pack-years, BMI), making the standalone PRS contribution harder to judge. Despite PGS001791 coming from a global biobank framework paper, it still has stronger directly comparable PRS evidence than PGS004695.

Both candidates align well to the target (retinal detachment) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores with only basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). However, PGS001137 provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R²=0.00663), which can be sanity-checked against the trait heritability ceiling and interpreted directly as PRS signal. PGS001833 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² and reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0218), which is less directly comparable and provides weaker, less standard evidence of discrimination. Despite PGS001833 having more variants and larger training N, the stronger, cleaner PRS-only metric evidence makes PGS001137 better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS001030 is better supported for the broad target trait “pulmonary fibrosis” because it matches the umbrella endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all pulmonary fibrosis) and provides clean PRS-only performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6252; PGS-only R2=0.0142) with basic covariates, which are directly comparable and pass the heritability-ceiling sanity check. In contrast, PGS004695 is specific to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (a narrower subtype) and, while it reports a strong association (HR 3.78 high vs low quintile) in a large EUR cohort, it lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R2 and comes from an exposure-focused study context, making its standalone PRS performance support less directly evidenced than PGS001030.

PGS001137 is the better-supported choice because it provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics for retinal detachment (PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R²=0.00663), with basic covariates and a heritability-sane R² (well below the local h2_obs ceiling ~0.004–0.005, at least not implausibly inflated). In contrast, PGS002040 has similar endpoint alignment (retinal detachments/defects mapped to retinal detachment) and a stronger structural method/variant profile (LDpred2 with 706,872 variants, larger training N), but it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² and reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.0276), which is less directly comparable and provides weaker standalone PRS discrimination evidence. Both are UKB framework-style scores, so the deciding factor is the clearer PRS-only metric evidence in PGS001137.

Although PGS001030 reports higher PRS-only metrics (PGS-only R2=0.0142; AUROC=0.6252) than PGS001791 (covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only R2=0.005929; no PRS-only AUROC), that advantage comes in the context of a sparse 51-variant snpnet model and a framework archetype; meanwhile PGS001791 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto; 910,439 variants) and is developed across many biobanks, which is a stronger structural/transportability package. Both use only basic demographic/PC covariates, so covariate leakage does not explain the choice; the decision rests on endpoint fidelity plus the stronger multi-cohort, genome-wide construction of PGS001791 versus the framework sparse UKB score in PGS001030.

The AUROC gap is modest, so confidence is Moderate rather than High.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), come from the same publication/cohort context (Cancer PRSweb; MGI; EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and have identical training (n=6,005) and validation size (n=5,500). Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes (training n=8,029; validation n=8,473), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Net evidence favors PGS000461.

Given this near-clone context, PGS000631 has slightly stronger overall discrimination signals in the selected validation record (higher full-model AUROC 0.636 vs 0.618; higher Nagelkerke R² 0.0478 vs 0.0365; slightly higher per-SD OR 1.651 vs 1.568), while PGS000632’s main advantage is larger training/validation size and a higher top-1% OR (5.14 vs 4.4), which is a weaker tie-break than the broader set of performance indicators.
