Both candidates are near-clones for thyroid carcinoma: same reported/phenotyped endpoint (“Thyroid cancer”), same EFO mapping, same GWAS-hits method with 10 variants, and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either. With metrics limited to full-model AUROC and effect sizes, PGS000631 shows slightly stronger validation signals (higher full-model AUROC 0.636 vs 0.626; higher OR per SD 1.651 vs 1.598; higher top-1% OR 4.4 vs 3.53) than PGS000630, while PGS000630’s larger training/validation sizes and mixed EUR/MAE evaluation are weak tie-breakers here. Differences are small and based on non-PRS-only metrics, so confidence is low.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (8,029), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same validation N (8,473), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not PRS-comparable). With performance essentially tied (full-model AUROC 0.589 for PGS000465 vs 0.593 for PGS000463; per-SD OR 1.457 vs 1.448), the small AUROC difference is likely noise; the only modest structural edge is PGS000465 having more variants (10 vs 7) and a slightly stronger top-1% OR (4.54 vs 3.74). Hence PGS000465 is marginally better-supported, but confidence is low due to near-indistinguishability and lack of PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI), same training size (n=6,005), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=5,500), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). Given that, the best differentiator is the within-family empirical performance: PGS000470 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.557 vs 0.524), higher pseudo-R² (0.0154 vs 0.00141), and stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.308 vs 1.09; top 1% vs rest OR 2.45 vs 1.48) than PGS000469. Although PGS000469 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with many variants, its weaker observed discrimination/effect-size evidence in the same setting makes PGS000470 better supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication and release date, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sample sizes, and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With endpoint fidelity and study context effectively tied, the differentiators are modest: PGS000461 has slightly better full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.599 vs 0.589; pseudo-R² 0.0304 vs 0.0282) and a higher variant count (13 vs 10), while PGS000465 has a higher top-1% vs rest OR (4.54 vs 3.51). Given the lack of PRS-only metrics and the small AUROC gap, this is close, but the combination of slightly stronger overall model metrics plus more variants favors PGS000461.

PGS000014 is better supported for generic type 2 diabetes risk because it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only R2=0.029) with basic covariates and a broad multi-ancestry evaluation set, while staying endpoint-faithful (Type 2 diabetes). PGS002026 comes from a UKB portability framework paper and uses an incident time-to-event endpoint (“Incident type 2 diabetes”) with only full-model C-index/HR reported (no PGS-only AUC/R2), making its discrimination evidence less directly comparable to standalone PRS quality despite larger training N. The full-model metrics (0.752 C-index) in PGS002026 cannot substitute for PRS-only performance, so PGS000014’s explicit PRS-only R2 and broader evaluation support give it the edge.

Both candidates match the target trait (type 2 diabetes mellitus) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC/C-index is not a clean differentiator. PGS002308 is from a disease-focused trans-ancestry T2D PRS development/validation study and uses a cross-ancestry shrinkage method (PRS-CSx) with broader GWAS ancestry inputs and higher variant count (1,259,754 vs 830,783), plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.96). PGS002026 comes from a UK Biobank portability framework paper (DEV EUR-only, UKB-based) with an incident/time-to-event endpoint and HR 1.81; despite large training N, the framework/portability archetype and incident-only packaging are weaker support than the dedicated trans-ancestry T2D study context of PGS002308.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and both are UKB-based framework-style scores with only basic demographic/PC covariates, so endpoint fidelity and leakage risk are essentially tied. PGS001306 is better supported on directly PRS-comparable performance: it reports PRS-only AUROC=0.630 and PRS-only R²=0.02036 (and these are well below the provided heritability ceiling, so they pass sanity checks), whereas PGS001855 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) and no PRS-only AUC/R², making cross-model PRS discrimination harder to assess. Although PGS001855 has more variants (1505 vs 179) and larger training N, those are weaker signals here than having clean PRS-only metrics; validation sizes are similar order of magnitude. Therefore PGS001306 has the stronger visible evidence package.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to thyroid cancer/thyroid carcinoma), come from the same publication and training cohort (MGI), use similarly clean basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics/effect sizes). Given that, PGS000630 has slightly stronger overall performance evidence in the selected European validation record (full-model AUROC 0.626 vs 0.618; Nagelkerke R² 0.0393 vs 0.0365; per-SD OR 1.598 vs 1.568), and it also shows broader evaluation ancestry in its metadata (EUR+MAE) whereas PGS000632 is EUR-only. PGS000632’s only clear edge is a higher top-1% vs rest OR (5.14 vs 3.53) and a different method label (P+T vs GWAS hits), but within this same-study, same-endpoint comparison the slightly better discrimination/effect-size package favors PGS000630.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate T1D). PGS001297 provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.77118; PGS-only R2=0.0912, below the h2_liability ceiling) but it comes from a known pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (69 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transportability. PGS004162, while lacking PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R2 reported), is from a biobank evaluation/ensemble-learning study and uses a MultiPRS/ensemble-style method with far broader genome-wide coverage (62,645 variants) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈2.89), plus larger validation (n=90,274) and multi-ancestry evaluation (EUR/SAS). Given the framework penalty and extreme sparsity for PGS001297, the overall evidence package favors PGS004162 despite missing PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to ulcerative colitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS004253 is better supported as a standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,575) and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.84, 95% CI 1.76–1.93), which is meaningful evidence of discriminative signal even though only a full-model AUROC (0.66) is shown and no PGS-only AUC/R2 is provided. In contrast, PGS001855 comes from a UKB portability/framework-style paper, uses a very sparse penalized regression score (1,505 variants), and provides only a modest PRS-comparable metric (partial-r 0.0625) without effect sizes; despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation and larger training/validation N, that framework/sparse construction is a consistent negative signal versus a disease-focused genome-wide PRS with strong OR evidence.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes). PGS001297 provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.771 and PGS-only R2=0.0912) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and its PRS-only R2 is plausible under the provided T1D heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.219). In contrast, PGS000024 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.921 with unknown covariates and no PGS-only AUC/R2, so its apparent advantage is not comparable and could be covariate-driven; training sample size is also not reported. Despite PGS000024 being disease-focused and having broad evaluation, the lack of PRS-only metrics makes it less directly supported than PGS001297 on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate T1D), and neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R², so the very high AUROC shown for PGS000024 (0.921) cannot be treated as standalone PRS evidence—especially with covariates listed as Unknown. PGS004162 has cleaner comparability metadata (covariates explicitly 0), provides supportive PRS effect-size evidence (OR per SD ~2.89 with CI), and uses a structurally stronger ensemble/multi-PRS approach with far broader genome-wide coverage (62,645 variants vs 85). While PGS000024 has larger validation size and more diverse evaluation ancestries, its sparse GWAS-hit construction and reliance on full-model AUROC without PRS-only metrics make it less well-supported as a standalone PRS than PGS004162.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo and identical phenotyping_reported “Cancer of bladder”), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so the full-model AUROC ~0.57 is not a strong differentiator). Given this, structural/evidence tie-breaks favor PGS000613: it has larger training sample (12,992 vs 7,469), slightly stronger top-1% vs rest enrichment (OR 2.91 vs 1.47) and better calibration proxy (lower Brier 0.0821 vs 0.0917), with essentially identical per-SD OR (~1.30) and AUROC. The advantage is modest, hence Moderate confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target urinary bladder cancer: same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported (“Cancer of bladder”), same method (GWAS Hits) and variant count (13), same EUR-only ancestry, same basic covariates, and same publication/date. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.572 for PGS000610 vs 0.567 for PGS000611) is not a strong PRS discriminator. With endpoints and metrics essentially tied, PGS000611 gets the edge on slightly stronger support signals: larger training sample (12,992 vs 7,469) and larger validation sample (13,530 vs 7,622), while PGS000610’s other metrics are not clearly better (e.g., weaker top-1% OR 1.47 vs 2.66).

PGS004253 is the better-supported ulcerative colitis PRS on endpoint/study archetype and PRS signal: it is from a disease-focused UC study (immune checkpoint inhibitor–mediated colitis context) using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto; 744,575 variants) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.84, 95% CI 1.76–1.93) with only basic covariates, which is meaningful evidence of PRS discrimination even though only a full-model AUROC (0.66) is shown. PGS001306, while it provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.630, PGS-only R2=0.020) and larger training/validation in UKB, comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“813 traits”) with a very sparse 179-variant snpnet model—an archetype that domain guidance flags as less reliable for external performance. Both have matching UC phenotype fields and similarly basic covariates; the decision therefore hinges on framework penalty + sparse architecture vs disease-focused genome-wide model with strong OR evidence, favoring PGS004253.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus”, trait_efo urolithiasis), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and multi-ancestry evaluation setup. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are the PRS-comparable metric available (partial-r) and structural properties. PGS002075 has higher partial correlation (0.0385 vs 0.0323) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (731,196 vs 5,599), which is a favorable structural signal for a complex disease like urolithiasis when other fields are matched. Therefore PGS002075 is better supported than PGS001864 on the visible evidence.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate T2D) and both use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array/site), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are essentially tied. PGS000014 has a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R²=0.029, below the h2_liability ceiling) and larger validation (n=288,978), but it is trained on EUR-only GWAS and uses an older single-ancestry LDpred construction. PGS002308 comes from a disease-focused trans-ancestry PRS study with explicitly diverse GWAS inputs and much broader multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME), plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.96) supporting meaningful PRS signal even though only full-model AUROC/R² are shown (not directly comparable). Given the target is generic T2D risk and transportability/robustness across ancestries is a key support signal, PGS002308 is better-supported overall despite weaker PRS-only metric reporting.

PGS001864 is the better match to the target trait urolithiasis at the disease-concept level: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are the generic diagnosis-style endpoint “Urinary calculus” mapped directly to urolithiasis, whereas PGS001250 is specifically “Calculus of kidney and ureter (time-to-event)” (incident/TTE framing and narrower kidney/ureter subtype mapping to nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis rather than the umbrella urolithiasis). Although PGS001250 has cleaner PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592) and a larger validation sample, it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”), which is a negative archetype signal for external robustness; PGS001864, while also a UKB portability framework and lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, uses a more genome-wide penalized regression with many more variants (5599 vs 341) and has broader multi-ancestry evaluation listed. Given the tradeoff (better endpoint fidelity/structure for PGS001864 vs explicit PRS-only metrics for PGS001250), the decision is close, hence low confidence.

PGS002075 is the better-supported match to the target urolithiasis on endpoint fidelity and structural properties: its trait_efo is exactly urolithiasis and phenotyping_reported is a direct diagnosis-style “Urinary calculus,” whereas PGS001250 targets the narrower “calculus of kidney and ureter” and is explicitly time-to-event (a mild mismatch for a generic urolithiasis target). Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.5668 / 0.00592), it comes from a pan-trait sparse snpnet framework with only 341 variants, while PGS002075 uses genome-wide LDpred2 with ~731k variants and is evaluated across more ancestries (including AFR/EAS/SAS/GME). Confidence is low because PGS002075 lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R², so the decision relies mainly on phenotype alignment plus method/variant-count signals rather than directly comparable discrimination metrics.

PGS001795 is better supported by PRS-comparable performance evidence and stronger structural properties: it reports a PRS-only (covariates-regressed-out) Nagelkerke R2=0.001948 (sanity-consistent with the low uterine-cancer heritability ceiling) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with ~911k variants, whereas PGS000542 is a very sparse P+T score (20 variants) and only provides full-model AUROC/R2 (0.572/0.0126) without any PRS-only metric, making its discrimination evidence less directly attributable to the PRS. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (uterine cancer/uterine carcinoma), and both use only basic demographic/PC covariates, but the combination of PRS-only R2 plus genome-wide construction gives PGS001795 the clearer, more comparable support despite its framework-style publication context.

Both candidates are near-clones: same uterine cancer endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported match), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same UKB training cohort and training N=7,131, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not PRS-comparable). With endpoints and design essentially identical, the only differentiators are small full-model performance/effect-size differences: PGS000541 has slightly higher AUROC (0.576 vs 0.572), slightly higher pseudo-R² (0.0133 vs 0.0126), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.311 vs 1.302), while PGS000542 only has a higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.6 vs 2.12). Given the overall near-tie and that small AUROC differences are mostly noise, I pick PGS000541 on the marginally stronger overall discrimination/effect-size package.

PGS001536 is endpoint-faithful to vitiligo (trait_reported vitiligo time-to-event; phenotyping_reported “TTE vitiligo”) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates only and an R2 well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs~0.17), supporting metric sanity. It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) and a large validation sample (n=67,425). In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is “anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients,” which is not vitiligo, and it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only an HR=1.41 and a meta-analysis p-value), making it much less supported for the target trait despite EUR-only evaluation.

PGS001795 is better supported as a standalone PRS for uterine cancer because it reports a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.001948; Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with ~912k variants, which is structurally more appropriate for polygenic signal capture than the 18-variant GWAS-hits score in PGS000541. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both phenotyping_reported are uterine cancer/uterus malignancy; EFO mapping differs only at the carcinoma vs cancer level). Although PGS000541 has cleaner/basic covariates and provides per-SD OR=1.311, its only AUC is full-model (0.576) and it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, making its PRS contribution less directly evidenced than PGS001795’s covariates-regressed-out R2; PGS001795’s reported AUROC=0.66 is likely covariate-influenced given heavier covariates, but the PRS-only R2 remains usable and is below the heritability ceiling. Overall, PGS001795 has stronger PRS-specific performance evidence and a stronger PRS construction despite being from a global-biobank framework paper.

PGS000738 is better supported for the target trait vitiligo because its study context and phenotyping are more plausibly aligned with vitiligo genetics (publication explicitly about autoimmune vitiligo and polygenic inheritance), whereas PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported is a treatment-induced, therapy-specific endpoint (“anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients”), which is a clear endpoint mismatch/packaging risk for generic vitiligo risk despite the vitiligo label fields. Neither candidate provides PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (both lack pgs_only_auc/pgs_only_r2), so metrics don’t rescue PGS000760; its HR=1.41 is only moderate and tied to a non-vitiligo endpoint. PGS000738 at least reports a (full-model) pseudo R² and is anchored in a vitiligo-focused paper, making it the more endpoint-faithful choice overall.

Both candidates are near-identical on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported Bladder cancer; trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma; phenotyping_reported Cancer of bladder), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), cohorts (UKB), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and training/validation sizes. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on within-family empirical performance/effect sizes and structural signals. PGS000613 shows consistently slightly stronger validation evidence than PGS000611: higher full-model AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher OR per SD (1.301 vs 1.284) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.91 vs 2.66). With otherwise matched design, these aligned improvements favor PGS000613 over the GWAS-hits sibling PGS000611.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS on the visible fields: it has coherent phenotype alignment (trait_reported vitiligo time-to-event; phenotyping_reported TTE vitiligo) and reports clean PRS-only performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), which are plausible under the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs~0.17). It also has clear basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, array) and a large, explicitly described UKB training/validation context with multi-ancestry evaluation listed. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata mismatch (phenotyping_reported="Red hair" despite trait_reported vitiligo), lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R2 (only a pseudo R2/full-model-style metric), and has unknown covariates and unclear training cohorts, making its support for vitiligo risk prediction much weaker despite the disease-focused publication title.
